title: The mysterious
hook: Einstein wrote that the most beautiful thing we can experience is the mysterious

segments.voice: Yesterday, Darwin's entangled bank, and the last word of his book. Your line was grandeur in this view. Did you find a tangled corner of life? Today, a physicist names what he thinks is worth the most. Day one thousand twenty-five.

What's the most beautiful thing a person can experience? Ask around and the answers come quickly. A newborn's face. A sunrise over water. Falling in love. A piece of music that stops you halfway up the stairs. A friend laughing at the kitchen table. Albert Einstein, the physicist, gave a different answer in an essay about what he believed. He said the most beautiful thing we can experience is the mysterious. Not the solved. The mysterious.
screen: `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING?` → `A PHYSICIST'S ANSWER.` → `NOT THE SOLVED.`

segments.voice: His words are paraphrased here, not quoted. First, the claim itself. The most beautiful thing we can experience, Einstein wrote, is the mysterious. Not a puzzle waiting for an answer key. Something real that we can sense but can't get to the bottom of. Second, where it leads. He called it the source of all true art and all true science. That's a surprise from a scientist. Plenty of people picture science as a machine for getting rid of mystery. He says the opposite: mystery is where the work begins, and where it keeps coming from. Third, what happens without it. Einstein wrote that a person to whom this feeling is a stranger, who can no longer pause to wonder and stand rapt in awe, is as good as dead: their eyes are closed. Strong words. Fourth, his religion. He went on to say that knowing something we can't penetrate exists, a deep reason and a radiant beauty that our minds can only grasp in their most basic forms, is at the heart of true religiousness. And then he drew a careful line: in that sense, and in that sense only, he counted himself among the devoutly religious. He was naming his own meaning of the word, not setting a rule for anyone else's.
screen: `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING` · `THE SOURCE OF ART AND SCIENCE` · `EYES THAT CAN STILL WONDER` · `RELIGIOUS IN THIS SENSE ONLY` · then, large: `THE MYSTERIOUS.`

segments.voice: The practice is to sit with one mystery. Choose something you can't explain and probably never will. Why a piece of music can move someone to tears. What another person's inner life is really like. Why the world can be understood at all. Hold it the way you'd hold a stone in your palm. Don't try to solve it. When the mind starts arguing, set the argument down, and go back to simply holding the question. The bell holds the time.
The mysterious. Einstein's name for what we sense but can't get to the bottom of, which he called the most beautiful thing we can experience. Today's word.
Your line: the mysterious. Today, look once at a face you know well, and notice how much of that person you still can't see. Day one thousand twenty-five.

howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, keep a practice of sitting with an open question rather than an answer, and Einstein's essay is often read as a description of that kind of wonder.

original.note: German, from Einstein's essay: the most beautiful thing … the mysterious.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mysterious means a puzzle nobody has solved yet.
what it means: what we sense but can't get to the bottom of, and the awe it stirs.
what a scholar hears: Einstein makes it the source of both art and science, and draws a careful line around his own use of religious: in this sense, and this sense only.

sources.ref: Mein Weltbild / 'The World as I See It' (essay)
sources.work: Albert Einstein, essay on what he believed

notes: Einstein is paraphrased throughout: English translations of the essay are not on the public-domain list (and the US status of the 1930s translations should be checked before any quotation).

Paraphrase follows the essay: the mysterious as the most beautiful thing we can experience; the source of all true art and science; one to whom the emotion is a stranger is as good as dead, eyes closed; knowledge of what we cannot penetrate, the profoundest reason and most radiant beauty, at the center of true religiousness; 'in this sense, and in this sense alone' he counts himself devoutly religious. Confirm against the German.
Original: 'Das Schönste, was wir erleben können, ist das Geheimnisvolle.' Confirm spelling and the pronunciation guide.
'People of many faiths mean more than that by religion' is meant to avoid presenting Einstein's definition as the definition; confirm it is fair and unranked.
Outline date (1930) left out under the claims rule; the hook keeps the outline's 'most beautiful' because the cited essay says it.

Editor pass: cut the filler 'He seems to mean them' and the sweeping 'people of many faiths' line; practice examples and carry changed so they no longer repeat day 1011's 'why there is anything at all' question and open-door carry; removed the unclear 'what happens to the light when the eyes close'.

Audit pass: paraphrase checked against the essay (fits both the 1930 'Mein Glaubensbekenntnis/Living Philosophies' and Mein Weltbild versions); 'You might expect him to say' (telling the listener what they think) changed to a general statement. The essay's English wording varies by translation ('source of all true art and science' vs 'cradle of true art and true science'), which supports paraphrase only.
